newsitem.title: UK: British budget must juggle expediency, prudence.
newsitem.headline: British budget must juggle expediency, prudence.

text.p: Britain's Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke faces a delicate balancing act between economic prudence and political expediency as he prepares to present his last pre-election budget in a week's time.

With the opposition Labour Party enjoying a stubbornly high lead in opinion polls, Clarke's Conservative colleagues will want him to do all he can in his November 26 budget to turn the tide and help secure them a fifth election victory.
Traditionally, this means the finance minister cutting taxes to smooth the way before parliamentary polls must be held by the end of next May.

However, Britain has a large budget deficit and underlying annual inflation jumped alarmingly to 3.3 percent in October -- two strong arguments for avoiding a tax giveaway that could stimulate an inflationary consumer spending binge.
Clarke must be wary of upsetting financial markets, which would punish any signs that he is departing from the path of economic virtue by driving up money market interest rates.

Most City economists predict only modest tax cuts, possibly with a headline-grabbing reduction in the basic rate of income tax to 23 percent from 24 percent, and a widening of the 20 percent starting rate to ensure poorer people pay less tax.
However, economists at HSBC Markets have sketched out what they believe could be a neat resolution to the Chancellor's dilemma.

"The centrepiece of the budget could be a forward plan for tax cuts covering several years, bringing the standard rate down to 20 pence," economists Roger Bootle and Jonathan Loynes wrote in their budget preview.

"It may not be enough to win the election. But the constraints are such that, in our view, it offers Mr Clarke his best opportunity of putting the Conservatives in with a chance of winning the election, while preserving the health of the economy and his own good reputation."

A programme of future tax cuts could also wrongfoot the Labour Party, which has moved to the centre of British politics under Tony Blair and is trying to persuade voters it is no longer the party of high taxes. It has so far been noticeably coy about its own tax plans.

Clarke, a rumbustious politician whose plain speaking has often got him into trouble with right-wingers in his own party, took financial markets completely by surprise on October 30 by increasing interest rates to 6.0 percent from 5.75 percent.

The move, intended to choke off future inflationary pressures, confounded conventional wisdom that the government would not risk alienating millions of homeowners by raising the cost of mortgages in the run-up to an election.
This strengthened his reputation for sound economic management, which he would not want to jeopardise with a risky budget.

The Chancellor has tried to dampen the usual pre-budget speculation, saying voters would be deeply suspicious of pre-election tax cuts after seeing the reductions before the 1992 polls quickly reversed after the Conservatives won.

Economists say the most that can be expected is a moderate reduction in income tax accompanied by cuts in public spending, resulting in a net tax giveaway of no more than three billion pounds ($5.03 billion) -- an acceptable figure for financial markets.

An added complication for the 1997/98 budget is that next year is the reference year for deciding which of the 15 member nations of the European Union will meet the Maastricht Treaty criteria for joining a single currency.

Britain has so far stood aloof of economic and monetary union. But Clarke, the leading Europhile in a cabinet divided over European integration, is keen to ensure that Britain meets the requirements on budget deficits and debt so that it could take part if it decided to. ($1=.5970 Pound)
